title: THE SMOKE WAS RISING. THE LIGHTS WERE FLASHING. BUT WAS GOD REALLY THERE?
paragraphs: THE SMOKE WAS RISING. THE LIGHTS WERE FLASHING. BUT WAS GOD REALLY THERE?
When Worship Begins to Look Like a Concert, How Do We Know Whether We're Encountering Jesus—or Just Experiencing an Emotion?
The lights dimmed.
A soft melody began playing.
Blue and purple beams swept across the sanctuary. Artificial smoke slowly rolled over the platform. The worship leader closed his eyes, lifted his hands, and whispered into the microphone:
“Church… can you feel the presence of God?”
And somewhere in the congregation, a woman began to cry.
A young man raised both hands.
Another person fell to his knees.
The music grew louder. The atmosphere became overwhelming. People were visibly moved.
But there was someone sitting near the back who wasn't raising his hands.
He was staring at the stage, wrestling with a question he was almost afraid to ask.
“If they turned off the lights, stopped the music, and removed the smoke… would we still know how to worship Jesus?”
That question deserves more than an angry Facebook argument.
It deserves an open Bible.
Because somewhere between the ancient altar and the modern auditorium, Christians have found themselves debating something that would have sounded strange to the early church:
Do smoke machines and stage lights belong in Christian worship?
Some believers see them as harmless tools that help communicate the Gospel.
Others see them as evidence that churches are becoming entertainment venues.
Some have been genuinely encouraged toward Christ in churches using sophisticated production equipment.
Others have walked away from such gatherings feeling emotionally stimulated but spiritually empty.
And both experiences deserve to be heard.
But there is something far more important than defending traditional worship or modern worship.
We need to know whether our worship is pleasing to the God we claim to worship.
And that question may expose something deeper than the equipment on our platforms.
It may expose the condition of our hearts.
Because the most dangerous thing in a church is not necessarily a smoke machine.
It is the possibility of creating an atmosphere that feels holy while neglecting the holiness of God.
Before anyone throws away the lighting equipment—or rushes to defend it—we need to remember something essential.
The Bible does not explicitly mention modern stage lights, fog machines, projectors, microphones, or sound systems.
It does, however, speak extensively about worship, reverence, truth, spiritual sincerity, stewardship, and the danger of replacing obedience with religious performance.
That is where this conversation must begin.
Not with nostalgia.
Not with personal preference.
Not with the size of a church's production budget.
But with Jesus Christ.
And the first place we need to look is not a modern sanctuary.
It is a well beside a Samaritan town.
A woman stood there carrying more than a water jar.
She carried a complicated history.
Broken relationships. Social shame. Questions about religion. A life that had become painfully tangled.
And standing before her was Jesus.
Not a celebrity preacher.
Not a worship performer.
The Messiah Himself.
When their conversation turned toward the proper place of worship, Jesus said something that would challenge generations of religious assumptions.
In John 4:23–24, He taught that the Father seeks those who worship Him in spirit and truth.
The original Greek contains a phrase that should make every worship leader, pastor, musician, and church member think carefully:
ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ
En pneumati kai alētheia.
“In spirit and truth.”
The word pneumati comes from pneuma, a word used for spirit, breath, or wind depending on context.
The word alētheia means truth.

Jesus was not presenting a formula for manufacturing a spiritual atmosphere. He was teaching that genuine worship is not confined to a particular geographical location or outward religious arrangement.
In John's Gospel, worship in spirit and truth belongs within the larger revelation of the Father through the Son and the life-giving work of the Spirit.
The woman was concerned about where people should worship.
Jesus directed her toward the One who makes true worship possible.
And that changes everything.
Because a church can have perfect lighting and still lack spiritual sincerity.
A congregation can have no instruments whatsoever and still be filled with pride.
A worship team can sing beautifully while their private lives contradict the words coming from their mouths.
And a believer sitting quietly in the final row can offer sincere worship without anyone noticing.
God is not impressed by what impresses an audience.
He sees what human eyes cannot.
Remember what God told Samuel when Israel was looking for a king?
In 1 Samuel 16:7, the Hebrew text includes these words:
כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב
Ki ha'adam yir'eh la'enayim, va-Adonai yir'eh lalevav.
The sense is that human beings look at outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.
In its original context, God was correcting Samuel's judgment about whom He had chosen to be king.
It was not a passage specifically about worship technology.
But its revelation of God's concern for the heart is profoundly relevant.
We see appearances.
God sees motives.
We hear applause.
God knows whether the applause has become an idol.
We see raised hands.
God knows whether those hands belong to someone surrendering to Him or someone seeking to be admired.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because some churches may have invested more effort into creating an unforgettable Sunday experience than into helping people understand the Scriptures they heard that morning.
But others may use their equipment responsibly while faithfully preaching Christ, serving the poor, making disciples, and caring for their congregations.
We cannot judge the spiritual health of a church by looking at its lighting rig.
We have to examine its teaching, its priorities, its fruit, and its faithfulness to Jesus.
And we have to be willing to examine ourselves.
Now consider something that often gets overlooked in this debate.
The Bible contains smoke, light, music, and extraordinary visual manifestations associated with worship and the presence of God.
At Mount Sinai, smoke rose because the LORD descended upon the mountain in fire (Exodus 19:18).
When Solomon's temple was dedicated, a cloud filled the house of the LORD so powerfully that the priests could not continue ministering as before (1 Kings 8:10–11).
Incense was also part of Israel's prescribed worship under the old covenant.
Psalm 141:2 compares prayer to incense rising before God.
And Revelation 8:3–4 portrays incense associated with the prayers of the saints.
But we must be careful.
Biblical descriptions of God's glory are not instructions to manufacture an imitation of it.
The smoke at Sinai was not a theatrical effect.
The cloud in Solomon's temple was not produced by a worship director.
And the incense prescribed under the Mosaic covenant had a specific ceremonial purpose that cannot simply be transferred to modern church production.
Those passages do not prove that smoke machines are forbidden.
Neither do they prove that smoke machines are spiritually necessary.
They remind us that God's presence cannot be reduced to a visual effect.
And there is an important distinction between using a visual tool and claiming that the tool represents a manifestation of God.
A fog machine may create a visible haze that makes lighting effects more dramatic.
It cannot create the presence of the Holy Spirit.
A spotlight can illuminate a preacher.
It cannot illuminate a spiritually blind heart in the way God's grace does.
A sound system can amplify a worship leader's voice.
It cannot manufacture repentance.
Those things belong to the work of God.
And no production budget can purchase them.
But here is another question we must ask.
If smoke and lighting are not automatically sinful, can they still become spiritually harmful?
Absolutely.
Anything lawful can be used unwisely.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 10:23 that not everything permissible is beneficial or constructive.
His words were addressing questions of Christian freedom and the good of others, not modern worship production.
Yet the principle matters.
The question is not simply, “Can we use this?”
It is also, “Does this help us love God and serve His people faithfully?”
Does the lighting help people see, participate, and focus?
Or does it turn the platform into a spectacle?
Does the production support congregational singing?
Or does the congregation become an audience watching professionals perform?
Are visitors hearing the Gospel clearly?
Or are they leaving with memories of an incredible atmosphere but little understanding of sin, grace, repentance, and salvation?
And perhaps most revealing of all:
Would the church still consider the service successful if the emotional response was quiet, but the Word of God was faithfully preached?
That question reaches into the heart of our worship culture.
Because tears are not always repentance.
Goosebumps are not necessarily spiritual transformation.
And an emotionally powerful experience is not automatically evidence that God approves of everything happening around it.
Human emotions are real.
They matter.
God created us with the capacity to feel deeply.
Scripture itself contains lament, joy, trembling, singing, celebration, and sorrow.
We should never treat emotion as the enemy of faith.
But emotion must not become the measure of truth.
A person can cry during a song and remain unwilling to forgive someone.
A person can shout “Hallelujah!” and still refuse to repent of dishonesty.
A person can be deeply moved by a sermon and forget its message before Monday morning.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:21–23 that outward religious claims and even impressive works do not, by themselves, prove that someone truly belongs to Him.
That warning should humble us.
Not because we can perfectly determine another person's spiritual condition.
We cannot.
But because Jesus repeatedly called people beyond religious appearances into genuine obedience and relationship with Him.
And sometimes the most powerful evidence of worship appears long after the music stops.
It appears when a husband finally apologizes to his wife.
When a young woman deletes the message she knows will lead her back into sin.
When a businessman returns money he obtained dishonestly.
When someone who has been hiding an addiction finally asks for help.
When a believer chooses forgiveness instead of revenge.
When a person who has spent years running from Christ finally kneels—not because the atmosphere is overwhelming, but because the truth has reached the conscience.
That is where the conversation becomes personal.
Imagine a man entering church on Sunday morning.
He has spent the week carrying a secret.
His marriage is falling apart.
His children barely speak to him.
He has been pretending to be spiritually strong while privately drowning in guilt.
He walks into a beautiful auditorium.
The lighting is excellent.
The music is flawless.
The transitions are seamless.
For twenty minutes, he feels something he has not felt in months.
Relief.
He closes his eyes.
He cries.
And then he goes home.
But no one has explained the Gospel to him.
No one has reminded him that Christ calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness.
No one has shown him the hope of reconciliation, the necessity of truth, or the grace available to those who come to Jesus.
He experienced a moving service.
But he still does not understand how to bring his broken life before the Savior.
Now imagine another gathering.
The building is simple.
The speakers occasionally crackle.
The lights are ordinary.
The worship leader is not particularly polished.
But the congregation sings about the cross.
The Scriptures are opened.
Sin is addressed without cruelty.
Grace is proclaimed without compromise.
Jesus is presented as the crucified and risen Lord.
And that same man hears words that pierce through years of hiding.
He learns that forgiveness is not something he can earn by pretending to be righteous.
He learns that Christ died for sinners.
He learns that repentance is not merely feeling bad about what he has done, but turning toward God in faith.
He learns that restoration may involve confession, accountability, and difficult acts of obedience.
For the first time in years, he stops making excuses.
And he prays.
Not a polished prayer.
Not something designed for a microphone.
Just a broken confession:
“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I need Your mercy. Please change me.”
There are no flashing lights.
No dramatic musical swell.
No artificial fog.
But something of eternal significance may be taking place.
A sinner is turning toward Christ.
And that is worth more than a thousand perfectly executed transitions.
Yet we must not draw the wrong conclusion.
The second gathering is not spiritually superior simply because its equipment is modest.
The first gathering is not spiritually compromised simply because its production is sophisticated.
A church with excellent technology can preach the Gospel faithfully.
A church with no technology can preach error, manipulate people, or cultivate spiritual pride.
The decisive issue is not the visual style.
It is faithfulness to Christ.
And there is a warning here for those of us who prefer traditional worship.
It is possible to criticize smoke machines while secretly worshiping our own preferences.
It is possible to condemn contemporary music while refusing to love the people who sing it.
It is possible to mistake familiarity for holiness.
And it is possible to defend tradition so fiercely that we forget the command to love one another.
Jesus confronted religious people who honored God outwardly while their hearts remained distant from Him.
In Mark 7:6, quoting Isaiah, He spoke of people honoring God with their lips while their hearts were far away.
That warning is not reserved for modern worship teams.
It reaches every sanctuary.
Every denomination.
Every generation.
Every believer.
A pipe organ cannot sanctify a proud heart.
An acoustic guitar cannot sanctify a proud heart.
A smoke machine cannot sanctify a proud heart.
Only the saving grace of God in Jesus Christ can reconcile sinners to Him, and the Holy Spirit transforms those who belong to Christ.
This is why we need more than a debate about aesthetics.
We need spiritual discernment.
In Colossians 3:16, Paul calls believers to let the word of Christ dwell richly among them as they teach and admonish one another with wisdom and sing with gratitude to God.
The Greek phrase ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (ho logos tou Christou) means “the word of Christ.”
The emphasis is not on creating an impressive sensory environment.
It is on the message of Christ dwelling richly within the community of believers.
That message should shape the songs we sing.
The sermons we preach.
The prayers we offer.
The decisions we make.
And the way we treat one another.
If the church's technology helps communicate that message clearly and supports the gathered congregation, it can serve a useful purpose.
If it distracts from that message, encourages celebrity culture, or becomes a substitute for faithful teaching, it needs to be reconsidered.
The same standard applies to every worship method, ancient or modern.
And we cannot ignore stewardship.
A church may legitimately invest in equipment that supports its ministry.
But leaders should be willing to ask whether their spending reflects biblical priorities.
Are the needs of vulnerable people being neglected while production costs continually rise?
Are pastors and ministry leaders being equipped to disciple people?
Are children learning Scripture?
Are struggling families receiving care?
Are resources being handled transparently and responsibly?
These questions do not establish a universal rule about how much a church may spend on technology.
They are questions of wisdom, accountability, and love.
Because the church is not merely a place where people attend an event.
It is a people called together in Christ.
A body.
A family.
A community of disciples.
And the gathering should reflect that identity.
Consider the believers described in Acts 2:42.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers.
Their life together included worship, generosity, shared meals, and care for one another.
They did not have modern lighting equipment.
But that fact alone does not settle whether contemporary churches may use it.
After all, they did not have modern microphones, printed Bibles, or livestream equipment either.
The deeper lesson is found in what defined their community.
They were devoted to Christ and to the life He had called them to share.
That is what must never be lost.
Because a church can fill a building without making disciples.
It can attract crowds without teaching people to obey Jesus.
It can produce viral worship clips without helping believers endure suffering, resist temptation, or grow in biblical understanding.
And a church can be so afraid of appearing modern that it fails to communicate clearly with the people God has placed in front of it.
Both dangers are real.
Both require humility.
And both should drive us back to Scripture.
So what should we say to the worship leader who genuinely wants to use stage lights responsibly?
We should not automatically accuse that person of manipulating the congregation.
Instead, we can ask whether the production serves the songs, the Scriptures, and the participation of God's people.
We can encourage modesty, transparency, and thoughtful leadership.
We can remind the team that their role is not to become the center of attention.
It is to serve the congregation as they worship the Lord.
And what should we say to the believer who feels troubled by artificial smoke and concert-style lighting?
We should listen.
We should not dismiss sincere concerns as outdated or judgmental.
We should take seriously the possibility that certain production choices can distract, overwhelm, or create misleading impressions.
But we should also avoid declaring something sinful where Scripture has not established that prohibition.
Romans 14 reminds believers to handle matters of conscience with care, although its original context concerns disputed practices such as food and special days.
Its principles should not be used to erase genuine doctrinal disagreements.
Still, it reminds us that Christian freedom must be exercised with love and humility.

Some traditions also hold particular theological convictions about which elements are permissible in gathered worship. Those convictions deserve serious biblical examination rather than dismissal as mere personal taste.
The church does not need more Christians who win arguments while losing charity.
It needs believers who love the truth enough to study it carefully and love one another enough to speak it graciously.
But there is one more scene I cannot get out of my mind.
It is not a scene from a modern worship service.
It is a scene from Calvary.
A hill.
A cross.
A crowd.
Soldiers dividing garments.
Religious leaders mocking.
A suffering Savior.
No worship band stood nearby to create an emotional atmosphere.
No production team coordinated the lighting.
There was darkness over the land, as recorded in the Gospel accounts, but it was no theatrical effect.
And there, in humiliation and agony, Jesus Christ gave His life.
The sinless Son of God bore the suffering of the cross.
The One who deserved honor endured shame.
The One who had done no wrong was crucified among criminals.
And through His death and resurrection, God accomplished the salvation that no human performance could ever produce.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is the center of Christian worship.
Not a stage.
Not a style.
Not a building.
Not a particular musical arrangement.
The crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And if we lose Him, it does not matter how beautiful everything else becomes.
We have lost the very One for whom the church exists.
Perhaps this is where the real scandal lies.
Not simply in the smoke machines.
Not simply in the lights.
But in how easily we can become captivated by religious experiences while resisting the demands of the Gospel.
We want to feel close to God without surrendering the sin that is destroying us.
We want encouragement without correction.
We want comfort without repentance.
We want the beauty of worship without the cost of discipleship.
And sometimes, we want to criticize what happens on a church platform because it is easier than confronting what is happening inside our own hearts.
But Jesus does not call us merely to have strong opinions about worship.
He calls us to follow Him.
To deny ourselves.
To take up our cross.
To trust His grace.
To turn from sin.
To love God and our neighbors.
To become disciples who make disciples.
And there is beautiful hope in that calling.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that we must somehow become impressive enough for God to accept us.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He meets us in our need.
He exposes what is false so that we can walk in truth.
He calls us away from the sins that enslave us and into the freedom of belonging to Him.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
Not because our worship services are perfect.
But because His grace is sufficient for those who come to Him in faith.
That is why our Gospel Warrior message matters so deeply:
The scandal of human sin is met by the grace of the Savior.
The broken person is not beyond the reach of Christ.
The hypocrite can repent.
The exhausted believer can return to the Lord.
The wandering soul can hear the Shepherd's voice.
And the church can continually examine its practices in the light of Scripture, turning away from anything that obscures Jesus.
So, do smoke machines and stage lights belong in church worship?
The most biblically responsible answer is that Scripture does not explicitly forbid these modern tools, nor does it command or spiritually endorse their use.
Their appropriateness must be evaluated according to biblical teaching, the theological convictions of the church, the purpose of gathered worship, the good of the congregation, and wise stewardship.
They must never be treated as evidence of God's presence.
They must never replace biblical teaching.
They must never become tools for deceptive spiritual claims or emotional coercion.
And they must never become more important than the people Jesus died to redeem.
The church does not need artificial smoke to prove that God is present. It needs the truth of Jesus Christ faithfully proclaimed and lived.
A church with stage lights can glorify God.
A church without stage lights can glorify God.
Both can also dishonor Him.
The question is whether Christ is being exalted in truth and whether His people are being formed into faithful disciples.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone trying to win a debate.
But as a fellow soul who needs the mercy of Jesus every single day.
When the music ends…
When the lights return to normal…
When the church building empties…
When nobody is watching…
Is Jesus still worthy of your worship?
Will you follow Him when obedience is costly?
Will you trust Him when your prayers seem unanswered?
Will you worship Him in a hospital room?
In financial hardship?
In grief?
In the middle of a marriage that needs healing?
When you feel spiritually dry and there is no emotional atmosphere to carry you?
Because worship that depends entirely on an experience will struggle when the experience disappears.
But faith rooted in Christ has a foundation that suffering cannot erase.
And maybe someone reading this right now needs to stop arguing about the stage long enough to return to the Savior.
Maybe you have been hurt by a church that seemed more interested in performance than people.
Jesus sees your pain.
Maybe you have been unfairly judged because your congregation worships differently from someone else's.
You do not have to build your faith on the approval of strangers.
Maybe you have been attending church for years while secretly feeling distant from God.
You can come to Christ honestly.
No performance.
No religious mask.
No pretending that everything is fine.
Confess your sin.
Ask for mercy.
Trust in the Savior who died and rose again.
And begin walking with Him in the truth.
If this article has challenged you, I would genuinely love to hear your perspective.
Please speak with grace. Behind every comment is a person Christ calls us to love.
Our desire is not simply to gather readers.
It is to help people become deeply rooted disciples of Jesus.
We want people to have access to biblical nourishment beyond a single social media post.
Resources they can read quietly.
Truth they can return to when life becomes difficult.
Encouragement they can share with someone who needs hope.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
You cannot.
They are not.
But because freely chosen generosity can become one meaningful expression of love for God and service to others.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
These items are not spiritual necessities, and buying them does not make anyone more faithful. They are simply resources and reminders that may encourage meaningful conversations about Jesus.
Because no ministry deserves the place that belongs to the Savior.
And no platform should ever become more important than the Gospel it was created to proclaim.
One day, the stage lights will go dark.
The final song will end.
The microphones will be silent.
The buildings we once admired will eventually pass away.
But the Lamb who was slain and who lives forever will remain worthy.
Revelation 5:12 portrays the heavenly declaration that the slain Lamb is worthy to receive power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing.
That is where Christian worship is ultimately directed.
Toward Jesus.
The Savior who carried our shame.
The King who conquered death.
The Lord who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And when you finally stand before Him, the beauty of your church's production will not be your righteousness.
Your only hope will be the grace of the crucified and risen Christ.
So whether your church worships beneath chandeliers, fluorescent bulbs, colored stage lights, or the open sky…
May the Word of Christ dwell richly among you.
May the Gospel be preached faithfully.
May sinners hear the call to repentance and faith.
May the broken encounter genuine compassion.
May believers grow in holiness.
May love be more than a song.
And may Jesus receive the glory.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be worshiping beneath artificial smoke—it would be standing in a room filled with light while refusing to surrender to the Light of the World.
